hook: Written by Croquembouche, this is an interactive file that asks you to accept an anomalous effect before reading, and it means it. Give it its full time and do not skip ahead, because the timing is part of the piece. If something seems to be missing, that is intentional.
whyItMatters: It belongs to the site's line of antimemetic stories, where the threat is something that resists being known or remembered. What sets it apart is that the reader's own experience of the page is folded into the effect, so the article enacts its subject instead of only describing it. The developer tools at the top are a rare, candid touch that lets curious readers poke at the machinery.
thingsToNotice:
The six-minute rule shapes everything, including how long you have before the text stops cooperating. Blanks sit exactly where the key word should be, so the document seems to forget mid-sentence.

The researcher's audio logs are the emotional center. He works out that the object turns into whatever each viewer expects, and its disguise turns out to be personal for him in the most painful way. His last questions shift from curiosity to grief, and the textbook excerpt at the end reminds us that the drug he took was meant to protect memory, not wear him down.

related.note: The classic object that cannot be remembered; the page links a story about it.
Another article that uses the page's own behavior as part of the scare.
